specStatements.text: Students should be able to explain how diseases caused by viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi are spread in animals and plants.
Students should be able to explain how the spread of diseases can be reduced or prevented.

Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. They may infect plants or animals and can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air.
Bacteria and viruses may reproduce rapidly inside the body.
Bacteria may produce poisons (toxins) that damage tissues and make us feel ill.
Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage.

Salmonella food poisoning is spread by bacteria ingested in food, or on food prepared in unhygienic conditions. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread. Fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea are caused by the bacteria and the toxins they secrete.

Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease (STD) with symptoms of a thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis and pain on urinating. It is caused by a bacterium and was easily treated with the antibiotic penicillin until many resistant strains appeared. Gonorrhoea is spread by sexual contact. The spread can be controlled by treatment with antibiotics or the use of a barrier method of contraception such as a condom.

Rose black spot is a fungal disease where purple or black spots develop on leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. It affects the growth of the plant as photosynthesis is reduced. It is spread in the environment by water or wind. Rose black spot can be treated by using fungicides and/or removing and destroying the affected leaves.
The pathogens that cause malaria are protists.

The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito. Malaria causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal. The spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.
Students should be able to describe the non-specific defence systems of the human body against pathogens, including the: skin; nose; trachea and bronchi; stomach.
Students should be able to explain the role of the immune system in the defence against disease.
If a pathogen enters the body the immune system tries to destroy the pathogen.
White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by: phagocytosis; antibody production; antitoxin production.
Students should be able to explain how vaccination will prevent illness in an individual, and how the spread of pathogens can be reduced by immunising a large proportion of the population.

Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection.
Students do not need to know details of vaccination schedules and side effects associated with specific vaccines.
Students should be able to explain the use of antibiotics and other medicines in treating disease.

Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. It is important that specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics.
The use of antibiotics has greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases. However, the emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern.
Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.
Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens.
It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.
Students should be able to describe the process of discovery and development of potential new medicines, including preclinical and clinical testing.

Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves.; The painkiller aspirin originates from willow.; Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.
Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry. However, the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant.
New medical drugs have to be tested and trialled before being used to check that they are safe and effective.
New drugs are extensively tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose.
Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals.

Clinical trials use healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial.; If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out to find the optimum dose for the drug.; In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know details of vaccination schedules and side effects associated with specific vaccines.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No vaccination schedule is named or dated anywhere in this set, and no side effect of any specific vaccine is described. The vaccination content is limited to what the specification requires: that small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen are introduced to stimulate white blood cells to produce antibodies, that a rapid antibody response prevents infection on re-entry of the same pathogen, and that immunising a large proportion of the population reduces the spread of the pathogen. Measles is used only as the example the specification itself gives for vaccinating young children.

concepts.definition: A microorganism that causes infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. They may infect plants or animals and can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air.

concepts.term: rapid reproduction of pathogens in the body
concepts.definition: Bacteria and viruses may reproduce rapidly inside the body, so the number of pathogens present can rise quickly after an infection begins.
A poison that bacteria may produce. Toxins damage tissues and make us feel ill.
Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage. This is how a viral infection harms the body, rather than by producing toxins.

A bacterial disease spread by bacteria ingested in food, or on food prepared in unhygienic conditions. Fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea are caused by the bacteria and the toxins they secrete. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

A sexually transmitted disease (STD) caused by a bacterium, with symptoms of a thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis and pain on urinating. It is spread by sexual contact. It was easily treated with the antibiotic penicillin until many resistant strains appeared. The spread can be controlled by treatment with antibiotics or the use of a barrier method of contraception such as a condom.

A fungal disease where purple or black spots develop on leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. It affects the growth of the plant as photosynthesis is reduced. It is spread in the environment by water or wind, and can be treated by using fungicides and/or removing and destroying the affected leaves.
The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. Malaria causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal.

An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without being the pathogen itself. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito, so the spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.

concepts.term: non-specific defence systems of the human body
concepts.definition: Defences that act against pathogens in general rather than one particular pathogen: the skin acts as a barrier; the nose has hairs and mucus that trap particles from the air; the trachea and bronchi produce mucus that traps pathogens and have cilia that waft the mucus away from the lungs; the stomach produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.
The body system that tries to destroy a pathogen if that pathogen enters the body, after the non-specific defences have been passed.
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: the white blood cell takes the pathogen into itself and digests it.

One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antibodies against the pathogen. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies.
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antitoxins, which counteract the toxins produced by bacteria.

Introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection.

concepts.term: immunising a large proportion of the population
concepts.definition: Vaccinating a large proportion of a population reduces the spread of a pathogen, because there are far fewer people the pathogen can infect and pass through.

A medicine, such as penicillin, that helps to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. It is important that specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.

A strain of bacteria that is not killed by an antibiotic. The use of antibiotics has greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but the emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern.

Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves. The painkiller aspirin originates from willow. Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.
The three things for which new drugs are extensively tested: toxicity, which is how harmful the drug is; efficacy, which is how well it works; and dose, which is how much of it should be given.
The stage of drug development done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals, before the drug is given to people.

The stage of drug development that uses healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial. If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out to find the optimum dose for the drug. In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo.

misconceptions.question: Are all pathogens bacteria?
misconceptions.correct: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease, and they may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi.
misconceptions.misconception: A pathogen is a bacterium, so every infectious disease is caused by bacteria of one kind or another.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet bacteria first and hear 'germ' and 'bacteria' used as if they mean the same thing in everyday talk. Bacteria are also the group most often drawn in textbooks, so the word pathogen gets attached to that one picture instead of to the whole group of disease-causing microorganisms.
misconceptions.correction: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. Measles is caused by a virus, salmonella food poisoning by bacteria, malaria by protists and rose black spot by a fungus.

misconceptions.question: Do bacteria live and reproduce inside your cells the way viruses do?
misconceptions.correct: Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage. Bacteria may reproduce rapidly inside the body and may produce toxins that damage tissues.
misconceptions.misconception: Bacteria get inside the body's cells and reproduce there, and it is that cell damage which makes you feel ill.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both bacteria and viruses are described as reproducing rapidly inside the body, and students merge the two statements into one. The phrase 'inside the body' is read as 'inside the cells', so the special feature of viruses is applied to bacteria as well.
misconceptions.correction: Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage. Bacteria and viruses may both reproduce rapidly inside the body, but bacteria make us feel ill mainly because they may produce poisons (toxins) that damage tissues.

misconceptions.question: Do viruses make us feel ill by producing toxins?
misconceptions.correct: Bacteria may produce poisons (toxins) that damage tissues and make us feel ill. Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage.
misconceptions.misconception: Viruses release poisons into the body, and those poisons are what damage tissues and make you feel ill.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Toxin is the first mechanism students learn for feeling ill, so it becomes the explanation for every infection. Students also hear 'toxic' used loosely for anything harmful, which makes it sound like the general reason a pathogen causes harm.
misconceptions.correction: Bacteria may produce poisons (toxins) that damage tissues and make us feel ill. Viruses cause harm in a different way: they live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage.

misconceptions.question: Do you have to touch an infected person or plant to catch a disease from them?
misconceptions.correct: Pathogens can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air, so contact between hosts is not needed for many diseases.
misconceptions.misconception: A pathogen can only pass from one host to another if the two make direct contact, so a disease cannot spread across a gap.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Direct contact is the route students can picture most easily and it is listed first. Water and air are invisible carriers, so students do not treat them as real routes and look for a moment of touching instead.
misconceptions.correction: Pathogens may infect plants or animals and can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air. The measles virus is spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs, and rose black spot is spread in the environment by water or wind.

misconceptions.question: Who is vaccinated against salmonella in the UK?
misconceptions.correct: In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.
misconceptions.misconception: People in the UK are vaccinated against salmonella, because vaccinating people is how the spread of any disease is stopped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other vaccination example students meet is a human one, so they assume the pattern continues. They also miss that salmonella reaches people through food, which means the sensible place to break the chain is in the animals that the food comes from.
misconceptions.correction: Salmonella food poisoning is spread by bacteria ingested in food, or on food prepared in unhygienic conditions. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

misconceptions.question: How does rose black spot get from one rose plant to another?
misconceptions.correct: Rose black spot is spread in the environment by water or wind.
misconceptions.misconception: Insects carry rose black spot from plant to plant, because plants cannot touch each other or breathe the fungus in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that mosquitos spread malaria and generalise that a plant disease must also need a living carrier. Because plants do not move or touch, an insect feels like the only way the pathogen could cross the gap.
misconceptions.correction: Rose black spot is a fungal disease that is spread in the environment by water or wind. It can be treated by using fungicides and/or removing and destroying the affected leaves.

misconceptions.question: Is the mosquito the pathogen that causes malaria?
misconceptions.correct: The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito.
misconceptions.misconception: The mosquito is the pathogen, so malaria is a disease caused by the insect that bites you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The mosquito is the only part of the story students can see, and control measures all target the mosquito, so it looks like the cause. The protist is microscopic and never appears in the everyday account of the disease.
misconceptions.correction: The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito, which acts as the vector. The spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.

misconceptions.question: What do the cilia in the trachea and bronchi do to pathogens?
misconceptions.correct: The trachea and bronchi produce mucus that traps pathogens, and the cilia waft that mucus away from the lungs.
misconceptions.misconception: The cilia lining the trachea and bronchi kill the pathogens they catch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that this is a defence system and assume that every defence destroys the pathogen. The moving hairs look active, so it is easy to imagine them attacking rather than simply moving trapped mucus.
misconceptions.correction: The non-specific defence systems include the trachea and bronchi, which trap pathogens in mucus that cilia then waft away from the lungs. Killing pathogens with acid is what the stomach does; destroying pathogens that get into the body is the job of the immune system.

misconceptions.question: Is engulfing pathogens the only thing white blood cells do?
misconceptions.correct: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by phagocytosis, by antibody production and by antitoxin production.
misconceptions.misconception: White blood cells defend the body by eating pathogens, and that is the whole of what they do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Phagocytosis is the one mechanism that is easy to draw and is usually shown first, so it becomes the image students keep. Antibodies and antitoxins are chemicals rather than actions, so they are harder to picture and get dropped from the answer.
misconceptions.correction: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by: phagocytosis; antibody production; antitoxin production.

misconceptions.question: Which do white blood cells produce to deal with bacterial toxins?
misconceptions.correct: White blood cells produce antitoxins, which counteract the toxins produced by bacteria.
misconceptions.misconception: Antibodies are what deal with the poisons, so a body flooded with toxins responds by making more antibodies against them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Antibody is the more familiar word and gets used as a general label for anything the immune system makes. The words antibody, antitoxin and antigen also look and sound alike, so students pick the one they have heard most.
misconceptions.correction: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by: phagocytosis; antibody production; antitoxin production. Antibodies act against the pathogen itself, while antitoxins counteract the toxins that bacteria produce.

misconceptions.question: Do the skin, nose and stomach protect the body by making antibodies?
misconceptions.correct: The skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, and stomach are non-specific defences that stop pathogens entering; antibody production is done by white blood cells.
misconceptions.misconception: The body's barriers work by producing antibodies against the pathogens that land on them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet the barriers and the immune response in the same lesson and merge them into a single defence story. Antibody is the strongest word in that story, so it gets attached to every part of it.
misconceptions.correction: Non-specific defence systems of the human body include the skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, and stomach. They act against pathogens in general. Antibody production, along with phagocytosis and antitoxin production, is how white blood cells help to defend against pathogens once they are inside.

misconceptions.question: Does a vaccine contain antibodies?
misconceptions.correct: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies.
misconceptions.misconception: A vaccine is a dose of ready-made antibodies, which are injected so that the body has them waiting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a vaccine leaves you with antibodies and reason backwards that the antibodies must have been in the syringe. The idea that you have to be given the pathogen in order to be protected from it feels contradictory, so the simpler story wins.
misconceptions.correction: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. The antibodies are made by the body, not supplied by the vaccine.

misconceptions.question: Does a vaccine give you a mild dose of the live disease?
misconceptions.correct: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen.
misconceptions.misconception: A vaccine contains a small amount of the live, active pathogen, so it gives you a mild version of the illness that then makes you immune.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'small quantities' is remembered but 'dead or inactive' is not, leaving the idea of a small live dose. Feeling briefly unwell after a vaccination seems to confirm that a mild version of the disease has been given.
misconceptions.correction: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection.

misconceptions.question: If most of a population is vaccinated, does that change anything for the people who are not?
misconceptions.correct: Immunising a large proportion of the population reduces the spread of the pathogen, so unvaccinated people are less likely to meet it.
misconceptions.misconception: A vaccine only protects the person who receives it, so someone who is not vaccinated is just as likely to catch the disease however many others have been.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Vaccination is taught as something that happens to an individual body, so students reason only about that body. The population level effect needs a picture of how a pathogen travels from person to person, which is a separate idea students have not linked in.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to explain how vaccination will prevent illness in an individual, and how the spread of pathogens can be reduced by immunising a large proportion of the population. With most people immune, the pathogen has far fewer people to infect and pass through, so people who are not vaccinated are less likely to meet it.

misconceptions.question: Will antibiotics help someone with a cold or flu?
misconceptions.correct: Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens; they help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body.
misconceptions.misconception: Antibiotics are the medicine you take for an infection, so they will work on any infectious disease including one caused by a virus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word antibiotic sounds like a general anti-life or anti-germ medicine. Patients often recover after taking antibiotics prescribed for something else, and viral illnesses get better on their own, so the medicine appears to have worked.
misconceptions.correction: Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens. It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.

misconceptions.question: When an antibiotic stops working, what has become resistant?
misconceptions.correct: Strains of bacteria resistant to antibiotics have emerged; it is the bacteria that are resistant, not the patient.
misconceptions.misconception: A person who takes a lot of antibiotics becomes resistant to them, so the medicine stops working for that person.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday phrases such as 'I have become resistant to it' put the patient at the centre of the sentence. Students also think of resistance as something a body builds up, like a tolerance, rather than as a property of a population of bacteria.
misconceptions.correction: The use of antibiotics has greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases. However, the emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern. It is the strain of bacteria that is resistant to the antibiotic.

misconceptions.question: Do painkillers cure an infection?
misconceptions.correct: Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens.
misconceptions.misconception: A painkiller makes the illness go away, so it must be killing the pathogen that is causing it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word painkiller contains 'kill', and students feel better after taking one, which looks like a cure. Most illnesses that painkillers are taken for clear up by themselves, so the medicine seems to have done the work.
misconceptions.correction: Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens. Antibiotics help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body.

misconceptions.question: Who or what is a new drug tested on during preclinical testing?
misconceptions.correct: Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals.
misconceptions.misconception: Preclinical testing is the stage where healthy human volunteers first try the drug.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word clinical is heard inside preclinical, so the two stages blur together. Students also remember that healthy volunteers come early in the process and attach 'early' to the earliest stage they can name.
misconceptions.correction: Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals. Clinical trials come afterwards and use healthy volunteers and patients.

misconceptions.question: What is a placebo?
misconceptions.correct: In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo instead of the drug being tested.
misconceptions.misconception: A placebo is a smaller dose of the drug being tested, given so that the trial can compare doses.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn in the same breath that trials start with very low doses and that some patients get a placebo, and they fuse the two facts. Low dose and no drug both sound like 'less', so the distinction is lost.
misconceptions.correction: Clinical trials use healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial, and further trials find the optimum dose. In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo, which is not the drug being tested.

misconceptions.question: What dose is given at the start of a clinical trial?
misconceptions.correct: Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial.
misconceptions.misconception: Trials begin by giving the optimum dose, because there is no point testing an amount that is too small to work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of a trial as a test of whether the drug works and reason that a working dose is needed from the outset. The purpose of the first stage, which is checking safety rather than effect, is easy to overlook.
misconceptions.correction: Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial. If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out to find the optimum dose for the drug.

misconceptions.question: Which plant does digitalis come from, and which does aspirin come from?
misconceptions.correct: The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves and the painkiller aspirin originates from willow.
misconceptions.misconception: Digitalis comes from willow and aspirin comes from foxgloves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two drugs and two plants are learned as one list, and there is no link between the names to hold the pairs together. Under pressure students recall that both pairs exist but not which goes with which.
misconceptions.correction: Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves. The painkiller aspirin originates from willow.

misconceptions.question: Was penicillin extracted from a plant, and are drugs still made that way today?
misconceptions.correct: Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould, and most new drugs are now synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry.
misconceptions.misconception: All traditional drugs came from plants, penicillin included, and drugs are still obtained by extracting them from living things.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Digitalis and aspirin are both plant drugs and are usually listed first, so students generalise the pattern to penicillin. The historical examples are memorable and get carried forward as a description of how drugs are made now.
misconceptions.correction: Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms; penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould, which is a microorganism and not a plant. Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry, although the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant.

options.text: A bacterium that causes an infectious disease
options.rationale: A student who treats pathogen and bacterium as the same word picks this. It is wrong because pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi, so naming only bacteria leaves out the causes of measles, malaria and rose black spot.

options.text: A poison that damages tissues and makes us ill
options.rationale: A student who thinks illness is always caused by a poison released into the body picks this. It is wrong because the poison is the toxin that bacteria may produce; the pathogen is the microorganism itself.

options.text: A microorganism that lives inside the body cells
options.rationale: A student who applies the virus mechanism to all pathogens picks this. It is wrong because only viruses live and reproduce inside cells; bacteria, protists and fungi are pathogens without doing so.

options.text: A microorganism that causes an infectious disease
options.rationale: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. They may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi, and may infect plants or animals.

mcqs.stem: Purple and black spots have appeared on the leaves of a rose bush in a garden. How is this disease most likely to reach the other rose bushes in the garden?

options.text: By insects moving between the plants
options.rationale: A student who assumes a plant disease needs a living carrier, as malaria does, picks this. It is wrong because rose black spot is spread in the environment by water or wind, not by a vector.

options.text: By direct contact between their leaves
options.rationale: A student who believes pathogens can only pass by direct contact picks this. It is wrong because pathogens can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air, and rose black spot is spread by water or wind.

options.text: By toxins moving through the wet soil
options.rationale: A student who thinks a released poison is what moves and causes disease picks this. It is wrong because toxins are poisons that bacteria may produce inside a host; rose black spot is a fungal disease spread by water or wind.

options.text: By water or wind in the environment
options.rationale: Rose black spot is a fungal disease that is spread in the environment by water or wind, so it can cross the gap between plants that never touch.

mcqs.stem: What kind of pathogen causes malaria?

options.text: A protist spread to humans by mosquitos
options.rationale: The pathogens that cause malaria are protists, and the malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito.

options.text: A bacterium spread to humans by mosquitos
options.rationale: A student who assumes every pathogen is a bacterium picks this. It is wrong because the pathogens that cause malaria are protists, one of the four groups of pathogen alongside viruses, bacteria and fungi.

options.text: A mosquito that bites and infects humans
options.rationale: A student who treats the visible biting insect as the cause picks this. It is wrong because the mosquito is the vector in the life cycle of the malarial protist; the pathogen is the protist it carries.

options.text: A virus that reproduces in human cells
options.rationale: A student who reaches for the virus mechanism whenever a pathogen gets inside the body picks this. It is wrong because the pathogens that cause malaria are protists, not viruses.

mcqs.stem: A health agency wants to reduce the number of malaria cases in a region. Which approach should it use?

options.text: Treating infected people with antibiotics
options.rationale: A student who treats antibiotics as the medicine for any infection picks this. It is wrong because antibiotics kill infective bacteria, and the pathogens that cause malaria are protists.

options.text: Stopping mosquitos breeding and using nets
options.rationale: The spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.

options.text: Vaccinating whole populations against it
options.rationale: A student who assumes vaccinating people is the control measure for every disease picks this. It is wrong because the specification gives the control of malaria as preventing the vectors from breeding and using mosquito nets.

options.text: Avoiding direct contact with infected people
options.rationale: A student who believes pathogens only pass by direct contact picks this. It is wrong because the malarial protist reaches a new host through the mosquito, so breaking that route is what controls the spread.

mcqs.stem: How is the spread of salmonella food poisoning controlled in the UK?

options.text: People are vaccinated against salmonella
options.rationale: A student who assumes every vaccination programme is a human one picks this. It is wrong because in the UK it is poultry that are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

options.text: Poultry are vaccinated against salmonella
options.rationale: Salmonella food poisoning is spread by bacteria ingested in food, and in the UK poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

options.text: Poultry are treated with strong antibiotics
options.rationale: A student who reaches for antibiotics as the standard answer to bacteria picks this. It is wrong because the control measure given is vaccination of poultry, together with hygienic food preparation.

options.text: People are given painkillers to cure it
options.rationale: A student who thinks a painkiller removes the cause of an illness picks this. It is wrong because painkillers treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens, so they cannot control the spread.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a non-specific defence system of the human body?

options.text: The nose produces antibodies to attack pathogens
options.rationale: A student who merges the barriers with the immune response picks this. It is wrong because antibody production is a way white blood cells defend the body; the nose traps particles in its hairs and mucus.

options.text: The stomach produces acid that kills pathogens
options.rationale: The stomach is one of the non-specific defence systems of the human body: it produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.

options.text: Cilia in the windpipe destroy trapped pathogens
options.rationale: A student who assumes every defence destroys pathogens picks this. It is wrong because the cilia waft mucus, with the trapped pathogens in it, away from the lungs rather than killing them.

options.text: White blood cells in the skin trap pathogens
options.rationale: A student who thinks white blood cells carry out all of the body's defences picks this. It is wrong because the skin acts as a barrier, while white blood cells defend by phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production.

mcqs.stem: Bacteria in the blood are releasing toxins. Which action of the white blood cells deals with those toxins?

options.text: The making of antibodies
options.rationale: A student who uses antibody as the label for everything the immune system makes picks this. It is wrong because antibodies act against the pathogen itself, while antitoxins counteract its toxins.

options.text: The engulfing of bacteria
options.rationale: A student who remembers phagocytosis as the only white blood cell defence picks this. It is wrong because phagocytosis removes the bacteria but does not deal with toxins already released into the blood.

options.text: The production of antitoxins
options.rationale: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by antitoxin production, and antitoxins counteract the toxins that bacteria produce.

options.text: The production of stomach acid
options.rationale: A student who mixes the non-specific defences with the immune response picks this. It is wrong because stomach acid is a non-specific defence against pathogens in food, not an action of white blood cells.

mcqs.stem: A pathogen gets past the body's non-specific defences and enters the body for the first time. What does the immune system do?

options.text: It produces toxins to kill the pathogen
options.rationale: A student who thinks of toxins as a general weapon in disease picks this. It is wrong because toxins are poisons that bacteria may produce to damage our tissues; white blood cells make antibodies and antitoxins.

options.text: It tries to destroy the invading pathogen
options.rationale: If a pathogen enters the body the immune system tries to destroy the pathogen, using phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production.

options.text: It develops resistance to the pathogen
options.rationale: A student who thinks of resistance as something a body builds up picks this. It is wrong because resistance describes strains of bacteria that are not killed by an antibiotic, not the response of the immune system.

options.text: It waits to be given a vaccination
options.rationale: A student who thinks protection has to be supplied by a vaccine picks this. It is wrong because the immune system tries to destroy any pathogen that enters; vaccination only makes that response faster next time.

mcqs.stem: What is introduced into the body during a vaccination?

options.text: Dead or inactive forms of a pathogen
options.rationale: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies.

options.text: Ready-made antibodies from donors
options.rationale: A student who reasons back from the antibodies a vaccinated person has picks this. It is wrong because the vaccine stimulates the white blood cells to produce antibodies; it does not supply them.

options.text: Live and active forms of a pathogen
options.rationale: A student who remembers 'small quantities' but not 'dead or inactive' picks this. It is wrong because vaccination introduces small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen.

options.text: An antibiotic that kills pathogens
options.rationale: A student who groups all disease medicines together as antibiotics picks this. It is wrong because antibiotics are medicines that kill infective bacteria already in the body, which is not what a vaccine does.

mcqs.stem: A large proportion of the population in a town is vaccinated against measles. What is the effect on the people in that town who are not vaccinated?

options.text: They are equally likely to catch measles
options.rationale: A student who thinks a vaccine can only protect the individual who received it picks this. It is wrong because immunising a large proportion of the population reduces the spread of the pathogen.

options.text: They are made immune to measles as well
options.rationale: A student who thinks the vaccine contains a live pathogen that passes on immunity picks this. It is wrong because only vaccinated people are stimulated to produce antibodies; the rest are protected only by reduced spread.

options.text: They are less likely to catch measles
options.rationale: The spread of pathogens can be reduced by immunising a large proportion of the population, so an unvaccinated person is less likely to meet the measles virus.

options.text: They must be given antibiotics instead
options.rationale: A student who treats antibiotics as cover for any infection picks this. It is wrong because measles is a viral disease and antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.

mcqs.stem: A patient has a viral infection and a painful sore throat. Which treatment is appropriate, and why?

options.text: Antibiotics, which kill the pathogen
options.rationale: A student who treats antibiotics as a medicine for any infection picks this. It is wrong because antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens; they cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria.

options.text: Painkillers, which destroy the viruses
options.rationale: A student who reads 'killer' in painkiller as killing the pathogen picks this. It is wrong because painkillers treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens.

options.text: Painkillers, which treat symptoms
options.rationale: Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens, so they are the appropriate treatment for the pain of a viral infection.

options.text: Antitoxins, which kill the pathogen
options.rationale: A student who uses antitoxin as a general name for something that attacks pathogens picks this. It is wrong because antitoxins are produced by white blood cells to counteract bacterial toxins, and are not a medicine given for a virus.

mcqs.stem: The use of antibiotics greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but some bacterial infections are now much harder to treat. Why?

options.text: Patients have grown resistant to antibiotics
options.rationale: A student who thinks the body builds up resistance to a medicine picks this. It is wrong because it is strains of bacteria resistant to antibiotics that have emerged, not resistant patients.

options.text: Antibiotics have started to kill the viruses too
options.rationale: A student who believes antibiotics act on any pathogen picks this. It is wrong because antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens, and this would in any case not make bacterial infections harder to treat.

options.text: Bacteria now reproduce inside human cells
options.rationale: A student who applies the virus mechanism to bacteria picks this. It is wrong because viruses, not bacteria, live and reproduce inside cells; antibiotics fail against certain bacteria because resistant strains have emerged.

options.text: Resistant strains of bacteria have emerged
options.rationale: The emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern, because those strains are not killed by the antibiotic that once cured the disease.

mcqs.stem: Why is it difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses?

options.text: Viruses live in cells, so tissues are damaged
options.rationale: Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, so it is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.

options.text: Viruses reproduce outside the body's cells
options.rationale: A student who has swapped the behaviour of bacteria and viruses picks this. It is wrong because viruses live and reproduce inside cells, which is exactly what makes them hard to attack without harm.

options.text: Viruses make toxins that destroy those drugs
options.rationale: A student who thinks viruses work by producing poisons picks this. It is wrong because it is bacteria that may produce toxins; viruses cause harm by reproducing inside cells and damaging them.

options.text: Viruses are easily destroyed by all antibiotics
options.rationale: A student who believes antibiotics act on viruses picks this. It is wrong because antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens, so this is not the reason antiviral drugs are hard to develop.

mcqs.stem: A pharmaceutical company has synthesised a possible new drug. Which describes the preclinical testing of that drug?

options.text: Testing on healthy volunteers, patients
options.rationale: A student who hears 'clinical' inside 'preclinical' picks this. It is wrong because healthy volunteers and patients are used in clinical trials, which come after preclinical testing.

options.text: Testing on cells, tissues and live animals
options.rationale: Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals, before the drug is given to any person.

options.text: Testing on patients at the optimum dosage
options.rationale: A student who thinks testing starts at a dose that works picks this. It is wrong because the optimum dose is found in later clinical trials, after preclinical testing and after very low doses have been shown to be safe.

options.text: Testing on some patients given a placebo
options.rationale: A student who thinks preclinical testing is the stage where humans first try the drug picks this. It is wrong because placebos are given to some patients in double blind clinical trials, which come after preclinical testing.

mcqs.stem: What happens in a double blind trial?

options.text: Some patients get a smaller dose
options.rationale: A student who has fused 'very low doses at the start' with 'some patients are given a placebo' picks this. It is wrong because a placebo is not a smaller dose of the drug.

options.text: Healthy volunteers are in the trial
options.rationale: A student who cannot separate the stages of testing picks this. It is wrong because clinical trials use healthy volunteers and patients generally; what defines a double blind trial is that some patients are given a placebo.

options.text: Some patients are given a placebo
options.rationale: In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo rather than the drug being tested.

options.text: Each patient gets the optimum dose
options.rationale: A student who assumes trials use the dose that works best picks this. It is wrong because the optimum dose is what further clinical trials are carried out to find, and in a double blind trial some patients receive a placebo.

mcqs.stem: Which drug is correctly matched with the source it originally came from?

options.text: Aspirin is extracted from the foxgloves
options.rationale: A student who has swapped the two plant drugs picks this. It is wrong because the painkiller aspirin originates from willow, and foxgloves are the source of the heart drug digitalis.

options.text: Penicillin is extracted from foxgloves
options.rationale: A student who generalises the plant examples to every traditional drug picks this. It is wrong because penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould, which is a microorganism, and foxgloves are the source of digitalis.

options.text: Digitalis is extracted from foxgloves
options.rationale: Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms, and the heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves.

options.text: Digitalis is extracted from willow trees
options.rationale: A student who remembers the two plants but not which drug goes with which picks this. It is wrong because willow is the source of the painkiller aspirin, while digitalis originates from foxgloves.

mcqs.stem: Why must new medical drugs be tested and trialled before they are used?

options.text: To check they are safe and effective
options.rationale: New medical drugs have to be tested and trialled before being used to check that they are safe and effective, which is why they are extensively tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose.

options.text: To check they kill bacterial pathogens
options.rationale: A student who thinks every medicine is meant to kill pathogens picks this. It is wrong because many drugs, such as painkillers, treat symptoms; testing checks that a drug is safe and effective for its own purpose.

options.text: To check they cure the illness
options.rationale: A student who thinks a medicine such as a painkiller cures the illness by removing its cause picks this. It is wrong because painkillers and other medicines treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens, so testing must check that a drug is safe and effective for its own purpose.

options.text: To check patients cannot resist drugs
options.rationale: A student who thinks patients become resistant to medicines picks this. It is wrong because it is strains of bacteria that become resistant to antibiotics, and testing is done to check safety and effectiveness.

mcqs.stem: How are most new drugs produced today?

options.text: Extracted from plants and microorganisms
options.rationale: A student who carries the historical examples forward to the present picks this. It is wrong because that is how drugs were traditionally obtained; most new drugs are now synthesised by chemists.

options.text: Extracted from the willow and foxgloves
options.rationale: A student who believes drugs are still obtained by extracting them from plants, and names the plants they have learned, picks this. It is wrong because willow and foxgloves gave aspirin and digitalis in the past; most new drugs are synthesised by chemists.

options.text: Collected from moulds growing in soil
options.rationale: A student who generalises the discovery of penicillin from Penicillium mould picks this. It is wrong because that was one historical discovery; most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry.

options.text: Synthesised by pharmaceutical chemists
options.rationale: Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry, although the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant.
